prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 topological insulator, and for its experimental observation in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: I opened with the Kardar-Parisi-Zhang candidate (B017) because it is the cleanest minimal model I know of for a non-equilibrium universality class. Reading the eight openings, I find that it has no support from any colleague, and the committee should not pretend otherwise. The topological insulator candidate (B036) is the one where my own scientific criteria and the committee's evidence converge. It is ranked by six members, first by Eriksson, and I ranked it second. The Kane-Mele Z2 invariant is a simple, general mechanism: a bulk integer that guarantees protected boundary states, in the same way I look for essential mechanisms behind messy phenomena. It was tied to a decisive measurement within two years (Molenkamp's HgTe quantised edge conductance, 2007), and the idea then spread well beyond electrons to photonics, cold atoms and phononics. That cross-disciplinary reach is what I mean by a universal result. Independent confirmation across HgTe, Bi-based materials and ARPES is strong and the interpretation is stable. The theory-plus-experiment trio is natural and the three-name limit is respected.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is overlap with the 2016 prize for topological phases and phase transitions, which Johansson and Lindroth both flag, and the contested credit chain: Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang predicted the HgTe effect, and Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore, Balents, Roy and Hasan and others built the three-dimensional story. A trio of Kane, Mele and Molenkamp necessarily leaves out contributors whom reasonable people would name. A second concern is that I am moving off my own first choice. B017 remains, in my judgement, deep science with a strong theory-to-experiment arc (Takeuchi and Sano), but its attribution is complicated by Parisi's 2021 prize, the role of the exact one-dimensional solutions is outside the credited names, and no colleague ranked it. A prize that only I would defend is unlikely to be a sound one.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B003 (ATLAS and CMS Higgs discovery) first as discovery by nature before theory, and notes that the credited trio are the founding figures of the experiments. For B036 he says Zhang's death in 2018 limits his eligibility.
responses.response: I accept the logic that nature should lead, and B036 does fit it: the HgTe edge conductance came after a sharp prediction, so I do not see Higgs as the only candidate in that mould. On B003 I share Lindroth's difficulty with attribution. The discovery was made by thousands, and naming three spokespersons or conceivers does not identify who made the physical discovery. That makes me hesitate to put it ahead of a case with a clean credit chain. On Zhang, I think the point cuts in favour of my configuration: the Zhang in the BHZ proposal (Shoucheng Zhang) is deceased and cannot be credited, which removes one of the strongest competing claims and makes the Kane, Mele and Molenkamp trio less arbitrary. I note that Yi-Cheng Zhang of KPZ is a different person and is alive, so that argument does not apply to B017.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B036 first as a clean theoretical idea (Kane-Mele with BHZ) linked to measured quantised edge conductance, mature for over fifteen years, with a natural theory-plus-experiment triad.
responses.response: I agree with the core of this and with the maturity assessment. I would qualify it in one respect: calling the triad natural understates the dispute. If Molenkamp is credited for the experiment, the citation has to say that the prediction (BHZ) and the observation are linked, and the committee should be ready to explain why Bernevig and Hughes are not named. I would also push on what the essential new idea is. I think it is the Z2 invariant and the bulk-boundary correspondence for time-reversal-invariant insulators, not the particular materials. That framing keeps the citation clear of the 2016 prize, which concerned integer-quantum-Hall-type topological phases and the Haldane model rather than the time-reversal-invariant Z2 class.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the optical lattice clocks (B025) first and magic-angle graphene (B022) second, and warns that B036 is partly covered by the 2016 topological-phase prize.
responses.response: I take the overlap warning seriously and have put it in my reservation, but I think the 2016 prize leaves room: it honoured Thouless, Haldane and Kosterlitz for topological phase transitions and Hall-type topological phases, whereas the quantum spin Hall effect is a different symmetry class that does not need a magnetic field. On B025 I agree that the physics is clean and the Katori and Ye credit is the clearest of any candidate. My difficulty is that it is a strong precision-measurement achievement closely adjacent to the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize, and I am not the right person to judge the atomic-structure side. I would be comfortable with it as a prize on its own, which is why it is one of my alternatives. If the committee finds it more mature and better attributed than B036, I would not resist.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B025 first because precision is what limits knowledge, citing fractional uncertainties near 1e-18, the redefinition of the second and relativistic geodesy, and thinks the 2005 comb prize leaves room for the clock itself.
responses.response: I find the argument that a new measurement capability opens other work persuasive, and for a theorist the lattice clock has an elegant idea at its centre in the magic-wavelength condition. Where I would press is the claim that the comb prize leaves room. Ye's record clocks rely on the comb, so the committee has to say what the new discovery is, as opposed to a long and impressive sequence of improvements in accuracy. If it is the magic-wavelength lattice and the many-body clock, the citation can say so, and then I agree it is timely. I would regard Kroll's case as the strongest competitor to mine, and I am open to a two-part prize, though with three names total the arithmetic does not allow Katori, Ye and the full topological trio.

responses.point: Pearce ranks the IceCube neutrino observatory (B007) first, weighing heavily the instrument achievement of a cubic-kilometre ice detector, and admits he cannot independently verify who was decisive among IceCube leaders.
responses.response: I agree that the instrument is a bold achievement and the discovery of a diffuse astrophysical flux is robust. My reservation is the same one Pearce states: individual source identification is still evolving, and the credit between Halzen, Spiering and the AMANDA and Baikal groups cannot be settled from the ballot. Danielsson also noted this point. I would put IceCube in a few years, when source populations are better established, rather than now. I would defer to him and Danielsson on particle and astroparticle detector questions, but I do not see enough maturity on the source side to rank it above B036.

uncertainties: Whether the 2016 prize leaves enough room for the Z2 time-reversal-invariant class, and how the citation should be worded to make that distinction explicit.
Whether the credit chain (BHZ prediction, Fu-Kane-Mele three-dimensional work, Hasan's ARPES) can be settled by the committee without arbitrariness, given that a trio leaves out several contributors.
Whether the committee would prefer a precision-measurement prize (B025) now, which would change my ranking only if colleagues in atomic physics show it to be better attributed than B036.
Whether B017 deserves a prize with Kardar and Zhang alone or with Takeuchi, given Parisi's 2021 prize and the lack of any colleague support for it in this round.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the shortlisted candidates. I have no recorded collaboration with any credited name on the shortlist. I work in statistical physics near the KPZ field, which is why I ranked B017 first, but I have not co-authored with Kardar, Zhang or Takeuchi as far as the profile shows. Johansson and Olsson are in the Gothenburg physics environment that is close to mine, with no specific collaboration found.
